result: Tolerable Upper Intake Level for adults 1000 µg/day of folate from fortified food or supplements, exclusive of food folate, also applied to pregnancy and lactation. No NOAEL could be set. LOAEL 5 mg/day from case reports of neurological progression in vitamin B12-deficient patients: more than 100 reported cases at 5 mg/day and above, and eight well-documented cases at 0.33 to 2.5 mg/day; in most cases folate maintained haematological remission. Uncertainty factor 5, chosen for the severity of the neurological complications and the use of a LOAEL; not larger because millions of people had taken about 400 µg without reported harm. A UL was set for all adults because the neurological consequences are devastating and irreversible, pernicious anaemia may develop at younger ages in some groups, and B12 deficiency in younger groups is uncertain. Dietary folate equivalents: 1 µg DFE = 1 µg food folate = 0.6 µg folic acid with food = 0.5 µg folic acid on an empty stomach; food folate bioavailability of about 50% rested mainly on Sauberlich et al. (1987), which was not designed as a quantitative bioavailability study, and 85% for folic acid with food on one isotope study, judged probably an underestimate. Under US fortification, it judged regular intake of added folate above 1000 µg unlikely in any group. The periconceptional trials of 0.4 to 5.0 mg were not designed to assess adverse effects, and adverse effects in long-term supplement users or in infants of supplemented mothers had not been investigated systematically. Hypersensitivity reactions are rare but have occurred at 1 mg/day. Folic acid is neurotoxic and epileptogenic in animals, without clear evidence of neurotoxicity in humans. Mental changes, sleep disturbance and gastrointestinal effects at 15 mg/day in one uncontrolled trial were not confirmed by other studies.
